lang.thema: ChatGPT Work: what the Free plan gets and when paying matters
lang.titel: CHATGPT WORK: FREE? WHEN $20 A MONTH MATTERS
lang.text:
A freelance designer opens ChatGPT on Free and finds no Work tab. So what's behind that door, and is it worth $20 a month?

But the strangest difference isn't the price. Here's what this video answers: what does paying for Work actually add, and who needs it?

Start with the heading that reads, Work is for paid subscribers only. Underneath, it says that right now, Work is available only to $20/month and up subscribers.

The next line settles it: Free users and $8/month Go users do not have access. So on Free, the Work tab stays closed. Bold design choice.

Scroll up and the heading says, ChatGPT Work is actually two products. Work Cloud runs through the ChatGPT website or the mobile apps.

Work Local comes with the ChatGPT desktop app, the one that used to be called Codex. The page adds that it can access files and run programs directly on your computer.

That's the first answer. Free has no Work, in either flavor. Paid starts at $20 a month.

Be sure to like, share and save this video.

Now the obvious question, in the page's own words. When should I use Chat, and when should I use Work?

OpenAI's official answer: use Chat for an answer, explanation, brainstorm, or short draft. Use Work for a clear outcome: a brief, deck, analysis, recurring update, workflow, or file.

The author's verdict comes next: almost entirely useless. A bold review of an official answer. Their reason: they've used regular Chat for all of those task categories for years.

So the author asks a better question: what features does Work have that Chat is missing? The page lists six.

Feature one: options to use Luna and Terra in place of Sol. In Work's model picker, you can choose GPT-5.6 Sol, Luna, or Terra. Each comes with reasoning levels: Light, Medium, High, Extra High, Max, or Ultra. GPT-5.5 is also listed, from Light up to Extra High.

The author's understanding from Codex: Ultra is a special mode that more eagerly delegates to sub-agents. Sub-agents are helper sessions that take pieces of a job. The page says these look to be the same models available through the OpenAI API.

Chat offers a different selection: 5.6 Instant, Medium, High, Extra High, and Pro. Extra High and Pro are only available for $100/month and up subscribers.

So $20/month subscribers cap out at High in Chat. And 5.6 Pro appears to be exclusive to Chat, with no equivalent in Work. The page doesn't say which model Chat uses. The author assumes Sol.

The last three: publishing ChatGPT Sites, and running sub-agent sessions with Sol, Luna, and Terra. Plus scheduled prompt automations, which the page says may be in Chat too.

Those are the six. The author calls one of them by far the most exciting. They're a long-time fan of the Code Interpreter pattern, which OpenAI pioneered in 2023.

So what does internet access change? The page says the code execution environment can now talk to the rest of the internet.

In Chat, the page says, that access is blocked by the container proxy. That covers installing software packages and reaching websites or APIs. Work can be configured with a specific list of allowed domains. But the default appears to be open to all. That's the strange difference: what the code can reach.

The page says you can have it clone GitHub repositories and install their dependencies, meaning the extra code they rely on. Then use them to interact with the rest of the web.

Another feature the page calls killer is the browser tool. Work can launch a full Chrome instance, load websites, fill out forms, and take screenshots.

What about sign-in? The page says the browser can prompt you to take over. You enter passwords and two-factor codes without round-tripping those credentials through the model itself.

It can even run JavaScript against the DOM, which is a loaded page's underlying structure. The author's own example prompt asked it to load a website and extract the headings using JavaScript. That test is theirs, not ours.

That's the internet half: code that reaches the web, and a browser that fills out forms.

So where do your files go when the chat ends? In Chat, each session gets a fresh filesystem that no other session can access.

In Work, each session gets its own scratch folder under slash workspace slash scratch. Those folders persist across sessions, so you can open files from previous chats.

The author counts 171 folders there right now. That's a lot of yesterdays. As far as the author can tell, that volume is mounted to all running Work sessions. File edits from one are instantly seen by the others.

Now the limit. The sessions don't seem to share the same process space, so running programs stay separate. Localhost servers running in one can't be accessed from another.

The second page is the Tool and Skill Reference. Its first line says tools are callable endpoints. Skills are reusable instruction packages that guide how those tools are used.

This snapshot contains 232 tool interfaces and 44 complete main skill files. It warns that availability can change with session configuration, permissions, connected apps, and installed plugins.

Hypothetically, a freelance designer needs a client deck. The reference lists a Presentations skill: read, create or edit PowerPoint or Google Slides decks.

Hypothetically, the same designer needs a quote table. The Spreadsheets skill covers spreadsheet files and Google Sheets, with formulas, formatting, charts, tables, and recalculation.

Then, hypothetically, a proposal document. The documents skill covers Word and Google Docs-targeted files, with a strict render-and-verify workflow.

Last, hypothetically, a portfolio site. The sites building skill is for websites, including landing pages and portfolios. A sibling sites hosting skill handles registration, publishing, and deployment verification. That connects to the first page, where publishing ChatGPT Sites is on the list of Work features.

That's a match on paper, not a result. We haven't tested any of this, and nobody should promise income from it.

Now the limits you can't see on a price line. The author believes Work sessions are billed against your Codex allowance. Chat sessions, they believe, get their own separate allowance. We have no figures for either allowance, so we can't say how far they go.

The author also wishes OpenAI had better changelogs. In January, Chat grew the ability to install packages, but that doesn't seem to work any more.

The page opens by saying OpenAI announced Work on July 9th and has been furiously iterating since. It calls Work extraordinarily confusing and very powerful. Rarely does one sentence sell and warn at once.

So here's the answer. Free and $8/month Go users do not have access to Work, in either flavor.

Paying starts at $20/month. The page's list starts with Luna and Terra options and a code environment with Internet access. Add a persistent filesystem shared between sessions, the ability to publish ChatGPT Sites, and sub-agent sessions. Scheduled prompt automations may be in Chat too.

Paying matters when a job needs a feature the page lists as missing from Chat. Internet access in the code environment, a persistent filesystem, or publishing ChatGPT Sites.

A client deck on its own isn't on that list. Hypothetically, a designer who wants files from earlier chats on hand does fit it.

One more caution about scope. The author talks exclusively about Work Cloud, and so have we. Work Local feels more like regular Codex re-skinned to be less intimidating to non-software-developers.

For a one-person business, start with OpenAI's task list. A brief, deck, analysis, recurring update, workflow, or file you can review and use.

Then hold that list against the features missing from Chat. A match means paying might matter. No match means it might not.

The honest limit: we haven't used it, and the page calls it extraordinarily confusing. Treat this as a summary of two pages, not a verdict.

Here's the part worth getting excited about. For $20/month and up, the page describes a tab that can complete a task. It also keeps files between sessions. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
